question: Part A. A social app stores 3 MB profile photos with each photo's owner and upload time. Where should each piece go?
options: The photo bytes in object storage under a key; the owner, upload time and key in the database
Everything, bytes included, in one database row
Everything in object storage, with no database row
The bytes on each app server's own disk
explanation: Object storage is built for large files written whole, and keeps copies cheaply; the database is built for small details you query, such as all photos of one owner. Bytes in the database make it huge and slow to back up, and files on one server's disk vanish with that server.

question: Part B. Why does a normal database index on the description column not speed up WHERE description LIKE '%shoe%'?
options: Because the word can be anywhere in the text, while a normal index is sorted by how the whole text begins
Because LIKE is not part of SQL
Because the table has too few rows for an index to matter
Because indexes work only on numbers
explanation: A normal index (SD 4) is sorted by the start of the value, so it helps with "starts with shoe" but not with "contains shoe somewhere". The database must read every description. An inverted index lists, for each word, the rows that contain it.

question: Part C. Orders are created on 6 database shards without asking one central counter, and the order list must show the newest first by sorting on the order ID alone, with no separate time column. Which kind of ID fits?
options: An auto-increment number on each shard
A time-ordered ID made of time, machine number and counter
explanation: Each server can make time-ordered IDs alone, the machine number keeps them from clashing, and newer IDs are larger, so newest first is a simple sort. Auto-increment repeats across shards, sorting by random UUIDs alone does not give time order, and an email is not unique per order.
